name: Confluence
tagline: A team knowledge and documentation workspace to evaluate for durable, searchable operational knowledge.
description: Confluence supports team documentation and shared knowledge; current plan details and independent ratings are not verified here.
pros: Structured spaces and pages can give teams a shared place for decisions and procedures.
A realistic search task can test whether employees can find trusted information.
Templates and ownership rules can support repeatable documentation.
A search test can reveal whether staff find trusted current information.
Page ownership and review dates can reduce stale instructions.
cons: Documentation becomes stale without clear owners and review dates.
Permissions and external sharing require careful governance.
Migration and export need to preserve links, attachments and page context.

content.title: Information architecture
content.body: Create a small set of spaces based on the audience and purpose, not the org chart alone. Define page templates, naming conventions, labels and ownership. Test whether a new teammate can find a policy, a project decision and a runbook without asking an expert.

content.title: Search and content lifecycle
content.body: Run realistic searches using the words staff actually use. Check duplicate pages, stale instructions and conflicting answers. Assign an owner and review date to important pages and define how superseded content is marked without breaking useful references.

content.title: Permissions and collaboration
content.body: Test editing, comments, restricted pages and guest access using accounts from different roles. Confirm that sensitive HR, customer or security documents are not visible to unintended groups. Review account offboarding and external-sharing settings.

content.title: Integration and migration
content.body: Test links and context with the tools used for tasks, code, service requests and chat. Export a sample space with attachments and verify how links, page history and permissions translate. Document what cannot be migrated automatically.

content.title: Adoption and total cost
content.body: Measure whether the workspace reduces repeated questions and makes decisions easier to retrieve. Include page cleanup, migration, templates, training, administration and plan-specific permissions in the cost model. Verify current product limits directly.

content.title: Pilot acceptance criteria
content.body: Ask a new employee to find the current onboarding steps, a project decision and an operational runbook. Measure whether they find the right page without guidance and whether the page identifies an owner and review date. Record duplicate or contradictory pages that need cleanup.

content.title: Failure cases and governance
content.body: Test a restricted page, an external guest, a former employee and a page that has been superseded. Confirm access and link behavior. Decide who reviews critical documentation and how old instructions are marked so users do not follow stale processes.

content.title: Decision record
content.body: Document space structure, content owners, permission groups, templates, search expectations, migration scope and export needs. Compare the time required to keep information current with the benefit of making it discoverable. Confirm current plan controls before storing sensitive information.

content.title: Knowledge-base fit and information architecture
content.body: Confluence is worth evaluating when teams need a shared place for decisions, procedures, project notes, and durable reference material. Start with the information people repeatedly ask for today and define an owner for each important page or space. Test whether readers can find a current answer using the navigation, search, labels, and page hierarchy that your organization plans to use. A large knowledge base without ownership and review routines quickly becomes a collection of contradictory documents rather than a reliable source of truth.

content.title: Page lifecycle and content maintenance
content.body: Choose several documents with different lifecycles: a frequently updated runbook, a project decision, and a policy that requires periodic review. Test edit permissions, comments, version history, page ownership, archiving, and how outdated content is identified. Agree on what makes a page authoritative and how superseded instructions are marked. A successful rollout should make it easier to identify the current approved answer, not simply increase the number of pages created.

content.title: Collaboration and connected workflows
content.body: If teams use Confluence alongside issue tracking or chat, test the full path from a discussion or task to a documented decision and back again. Confirm which integrations, automation rules, permissions, and cross-product features are available on the actual plans. Check what happens when a user can access a linked issue but not the source page. Do not assume shared vendor branding guarantees identical permissions or feature availability across separate subscriptions.

content.title: Security, access, and governance
content.body: Map public, internal, confidential, and restricted information before creating spaces. Test guest access, external sharing, group membership, search visibility, export, retention, and offboarding with a non-administrator account. Review the current vendor security and privacy documentation and contractual terms for the organization's requirements. Avoid storing sensitive records until the intended permissions and data-handling controls have been checked in the live configuration.

content.title: Pricing and adoption checklist
content.body: Current Confluence pricing and plan limits are not independently verified here. Check the official pricing page for user tiers, storage, automation, guest permissions, administration, and the features needed by the team. Pilot with a small group and measure search success, stale-page rate, repeat questions, and time to publish a useful page. No numeric editorial score is asserted until an evidence-backed scorecard is recorded.

faqs.question: Who should evaluate Confluence?
faqs.answer: Evaluate Confluence when its primary workflow matches a documented requirement. Test a representative task and verify current capabilities and limits directly with the vendor.

faqs.question: How should a team test Confluence?
faqs.answer: Use the same real input, expected outcome and acceptance criteria each time. Record pass, partial pass, fail or unknown, including setup time, manual work and failure handling.

faqs.question: Which limitations should be checked in Confluence?
faqs.answer: Check the exact plan, integrations, permissions, export, data retention, recovery and ongoing administration. Treat untested or undocumented capabilities as unknown until confirmed.

faqs.question: Are Confluence prices and ratings independently verified here?
faqs.answer: No. Current prices, plan limits and independent ratings are not verified in this review. Check official documentation and obtain a dated quote before purchase.

faqs.question: What should be confirmed before adopting Confluence?
faqs.answer: Confirm the core workflow, access controls, integrations, data export, account offboarding, support responsibilities and renewal terms. Assign an owner for the implementation and ongoing review.

author: Sarah Chen
learningCurve: Steep — requires dedicated training time for full proficiency
whoShouldUse: Confluence is ideal for small to mid-size teams that need a reliable project management solution without excessive complexity. It works well for organizations with 5-200 users who prioritize ease of use and quick deployment.
whoShouldNotUse: Confluence may be overwhelming for users who only need basic project management functionality. Its extensive feature set can create unnecessary complexity for simple use cases.
